The Semantic Web has successfully established a widely accepted query language, SPARQL, which is used to extract data from various RDF sources. However, the Semantic Web primarily deals with symbolic data, whereas the Web is increasingly becoming more visual. To address this, we propose VGStore, a system that extends SPARQL to handle visual queries over RDF data. VGStore introduces a new type of triple pattern, VGSP, which enables the querying of visual data, and supports a range of visual SPARQL queries. By integrating VGStore with existing SPARQL systems, we can leverage VGStore queries within a unified query framework. We have successfully implemented VGStore on top of Virtuoso, a well-known SPARQL system, and demonstrated its ability to handle visual queries over RDF data. Our experiments show that VGStore can efficiently execute visual queries, and even outperform pure SPARQL systems in certain cases. We believe that VGStore will play a crucial role in advancing the Web of Data and enabling the Web of Data to better support visual queries. By doing so, VGStore will help to bridge the gap between the Semantic Web and the Web, and ultimately create a more comprehensive and interconnected Web. We present a novel circuit improvement method that leverages SAT solving to identify potential enhancements for digital circuits. The method commences by deriving a set of constraints from the initial circuit design, which are subsequently used to discover additional valid gate configurations through SAT solving. Upon obtaining enhanced gate configurations via the SAT solver, these are seamlessly integrated into the original circuit. Notably, our approach is adaptable to various digital circuit designs and can be easily tailored to prioritize specific constraints, thereby facilitating the discovery of optimal enhancements. Moreover, our experimental findings demonstrate that the SAT-based enhancement technique outperforms existing optimization techniques, including evolution-based methods, in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Specifically, our approach consistently yields superior results, achieving enhancements of up to 100% and average improvements of 20-30% in performance metrics. Furthermore, our technique exhibits scalability, successfully enhancing larger circuits, which comprise hundreds of gates, and can be accomplished within a relatively short period of time, approximately 1-2 minutes. By analyzing the differences between distorted and haze-free images, our approach can be applied to a wide range of image dehazing methods without needing ground truth references. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed metric performs better than other FR-to-NR methods in predicting human visual quality. This research focuses on developing a simulation model for the p-PC Ge Detector's pulse form, essential for identifying the extremely low-energy interactions of interest. By utilizing the GRETINA detector simulation code, the study created a pulse shape simulation that incorporates the effects of charge carrier screening, phonon emission, and detector electronics. This simulation was then compared to experimental data from an 8.5 keV calibration source, yielding satisfactory results. This research will serve as a foundation for the Majorona Demonstrator's data analysis and will be further discussed in the paper. The simulation code is available for public use. Deep learning-based survival models have become increasingly prominent in medical research, particularly in predicting cancer patient survival outcomes. However, the lack of interpretability tools hinders their adoption in real-world applications. To address this issue, we propose the Inverse Survival Model (RSM), a novel pipeline that facilitates the interpretation of survival predictions. By leveraging the existing predictions, RSM enables the identification of the most influential features and the creation of a survival model that closely resembles the deep learning model. We demonstrate the efficacy of RSM through its application to the DeepHit model, a deep learning-based survival model. We evaluate RSM's performance using a breast cancer dataset and compare it to the existing explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques, such as DeepHit, DeepSHARK, and L0GD. The results indicate that RSM outperforms these methods in terms of explanation accuracy and robustness. Moreover, RSM's explanations are more comprehensible than those produced by other techniques, allowing for the identification of the most influential features. In conclusion, RSM's ability to provide reliable and understandable explanations makes it a valuable tool for deep survival models. The increasing complexity of power systems demands the use of advanced machine learning techniques to optimize planning and operations. However, these methods require substantial computational resources. A novel approach is presented, leveraging a deep autoencoder to efficiently decrease the dimensionality of power system data. This enables the development of more accurate and computationally affordable machine learning models. The autoencoder's encoder is trained to identify the most critical variables, which are then used to train a supervised learning classifier. The resulting model is capable of making reliable predictions on a full power system framework. The proposed method is successfully demonstrated on the IEEE 118-bus system, showcasing its potential to enhance machine learning-based planning and operations. The findings indicate that the autoencoder-based approach outperforms traditional methods, offering a promising solution for tackling the growing size and complexity of power systems. We investigate thermal properties of a four-dimensional causal diamond in anti-de Sitter space by analyzing the asymptotic behavior of its associated conformal frame. This analysis reveals that the thermal entropy of the diamond spans a finite range, approximately $\frac{L^2}{4\pi}$, within the weak curvature regime. Furthermore, we derive a precise formula for the entropy of a single conformal frame, which is expressed as $\frac{L^2}{4\pi}\left(1+\frac{c^2L^2}{60}\right)$. Additionally, we calculate the relative entropy between two causal diamonds and show that it remains non-negative. This result is then generalized to arbitrary dimensions and dimensions with a non-zero cosmological constant. We also examine the entropy of a single diamond in de Sitter space and find that it diverges in the weak curvature regime. However, we demonstrate that the relative entropy between two causal diamonds remains finite and non-negative. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the holographic entropy paradox. The full calculations for relative entropy are presented in appendices A and B. Counterfactual quantum cryptography, a protocol utilizing post-selection, has garnered significant attention due to its potential for secure quantum communication over long distances without the need for entanglement or sophisticated equipment. A variant of this protocol, cQKD, was recently developed by Sun et al. This paper examines the security of cQCKD within a real-world scenario where the sender and receiver employ distinct, non-ideal detectors. We demonstrate that an adversary eavesdropping on the communication can compromise the key with a remarkably low detection error rate, even when the sender and receiver are unaware of this breach. This finding highlights a critical vulnerability in the security of cQCKD within practical settings. A critical issue in the Internet of Things (IoT) is safeguarding user privacy, which is particularly challenging for location-based services that require users to share their precise locations. To address this problem, a recent solution leverages edge computing to enhance privacy by processing data locally, reducing the need for users to reveal their locations to service providers. However, this approach has its limitations, as it still relies on users' implicit involvement in data processing. To mitigate this limitation, a new protocol called the Edge-based Privacy-preserving Location-oriented Service (E-PLS) has been proposed. E-PLS enables users to share location information with service providers without revealing their actual locations, using edge nodes to perform necessary computations. Furthermore, a new cryptographic technique called the Edge-based Privacy-preserving Location-oriented Service (E-PLS) cryptosystem has been developed to enhance the E-PLS protocol. E-PLS achieves improved security and efficiency by leveraging edge nodes to perform complex operations, including key generation and verification. Notably, a formal security proof for E-PLS has been provided, demonstrating its robustness. Performance evaluations have shown that E-PLS outperforms existing solutions in terms of security and efficiency. Finally, a prototype implementation of E-PLS has been developed and tested on a real-world edge computing platform. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of E-PLS in practical applications. Deep learning models are frequently plagued by the issue of dead pixels in their output, resulting from the training process. This paper presents a novel method for quantitatively assessing the impact of dead pixels on model performance. By defining the concept of the effective receptive field, we develop a more comprehensive understanding of how this field influences model output. Through empirical analysis of pre-trained convolutional neural networks, we demonstrate the relationship between the effective receptive field and the location of dead pixels. Our findings indicate that dead pixels can significantly impair model performance, and we validate this conclusion by testing the models with intentionally introduced dead pixels. Our proposed approach provides a more accurate and efficient means of evaluating the effect of dead pixels on model performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential for our method to facilitate the development of more robust models by identifying and addressing dead pixels. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are increasingly being used in various applications, such as autonomous vehicles and augmented reality, which require real-time processing. However, the high computational demands of DNNs pose a significant challenge, particularly in battery-powered devices. To address this issue, researchers have proposed edge/cloud collaboration, which offloads computations to cloud-based servers. Nevertheless, the high cost of cloud-based approaches has led to the development of alternative solutions, which often compromise model accuracy. To address these limitations, we introduce AppealNet, a highly efficient edge/cloud collaborative architecture that optimally allocates computations between devices and the cloud. AppealNet employs a reinforcement learning-based approach to determine which layers should be processed at the edge and which at the cloud, based on the available resources. By doing so, it strikes a balance between model accuracy and energy efficiency, which is further enhanced by a dynamic re-allocation mechanism that adjusts the workload distribution in real-time based on the available resources. AppealNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches by achieving a 10% improvement in energy efficiency, a 20% reduction in latency, and a 10% increase in accuracy. The primary goal of semi-supervised learning is to leverage a substantial amount of unlabeled data to enhance the performance of a deep neural network. Current methods for semi-supervised learning typically employ pseudo labeling, which involves assigning labels to unlabeled data based on the model's current classification capabilities. However, pseudo labeling often yields inconsistent results, especially when the model is initially inaccurate. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called curriculum pseudo labeling, which dynamically adjusts the pseudo labeling process by prioritizing samples with more accurate labels. Our proposed method, FlexMatch, incorporates curriculum pseudo labeling and matching, as well as a novel loss function that incorporates a contrastive loss. Experimental results demonstrate that FlexMatch surpasses existing semi-supervised learning methods, achieving notable improvements in accuracy on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1000. Furthermore, FlexMatch exhibits exceptional performance in low-data scenarios, outpacing state-of-the-art methods that rely on transfer learning and meta-learning. The primary objective of Language Model Trajectory Prediction (LMP) is to forecast the sequence of tokens that a language model is likely to generate next, given a context and the preceding tokens. LATTE is built upon the foundation of a conventional language model, such as GPT-2, and it incorporates a transformer-based architecture that predicts the trajectory of language model outputs. LATTE's architecture is composed of a transformer encoder that processes the context and the preceding tokens, and a transformer decoder that generates the future token sequence. LATTE's performance is evaluated using the BLEU score, and it is compared with conventional language models. Our results demonstrate that LATTE is capable of generating more accurate predictions than conventional language models. Furthermore, LATTE's performance is comparable to that of a conventional language model when it is trained on the future token sequence. Our research also reveals that LATTE's performance is sensitive to the choice of the language model. Notably, LATTE's performance is enhanced when it is trained on the future token sequence. Our study also highlights the importance of timely vulnerability disclosure and highlights areas for improvement in both systems. Ultimately, our research underscores the need for a centralized security framework to ensure the integrity of open-source software. process behind each answer. This system is designed to provide transparent and
truthful explanations, unlike existing methods that often produce opaque and

unique evaluation process that assesses the credibility of generated explanations,
preventing it from favoring simplicity over accuracy. To evaluate Entailer's
performance, we developed a new metric that measures the quality of written
reasoning chains, taking into account both the credibility of individual steps and
their overall coherence. Our experiments demonstrate that Entailer outperforms the
current state-of-the-art models in providing reliable and truthful explanations,
resulting in higher user trust and acceptance. To facilitate further research,
we will release the Entailer model and associated data, allowing us to conduct a
more comprehensive analysis of its effectiveness. To the best of our knowledge,
this is the first system of its kind to prioritize credibility and truthfulness in
reasoning chains, providing users with a more reliable and trustworthy experience.

The COVID-19 pandemic has placed a significant strain on healthcare systems, particularly on emergency medical services. This research aims to identify the underlying factors driving an increase in EMS calls related to COVID-19 patients. We discovered that the EMS calls for COVID-19 patients are strongly linked to the daily hospitalization numbers, which suggests that the increased calls are largely due to patients being transferred from hospitals for further treatment in their homes. This finding has important implications for EMS and public health policymakers who can use these insights to prepare for potential future spikes in calls. This study introduces a novel approach to diagnose respiratory insufficiency in COVID-19 patients through audio data analysis. Building on existing research, we refine and expand audio feature analysis by incorporating MFCC-gram models, which surpass traditional MFCC analysis. Our method involves training a binary classifier on the refined feature set, yielding a 0.93 AUC score on the test dataset of the COVID-19 Chest X-Ray Images dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our audio feature analysis technique is effective in identifying patients with severe COVID-19, with no need for manual transcription or labeling. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of our model on the COVID-19 Audio Corpus dataset, achieving a 0.9 AUC score. Our findings suggest that audio feature analysis can be a reliable tool for early detection and diagnosis of severe COVID-19, with potential for wider application in respiratory disease diagnosis. Active learning strategies aim to optimize the use of labeled data by selectively querying its most valuable and informative instances. However, traditional approaches focus on reducing the number of labels required for a specific model to achieve a certain level of performance. In contrast, this work redefines the goal of active learning as improving the overall test performance, rather than just minimizing label requirements. To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach that dynamically boosts the test performance of a model through a process of iterative refinement. Our method involves identifying the most challenging instances misclassified by the current model and using them to update the model, thereby enhancing its test performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments on various datasets and models, and show that it outperforms existing active learning methods in terms of both test performance and efficiency. Our findings suggest that active learning can be used to improve the robustness of models to adversarial attacks, and we provide a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon. We have developed a novel algorithm that optimizes resource allocation and path establishment, and our simulation results demonstrate that this approach can reduce network resource usage by up to 30% and minimize traffic congestion, outperforming traditional methods. Furthermore, the proposed architecture can handle complex mission-critical services with high reliability requirements, and its scalability is not compromised, even with the addition of more services. Our research provides a solid foundation for the development of next-generation deterministic networking technologies. In high-energy physics research, the task of particle reconstruction involves grouping nearby calorimeter and tracker hits into individual particles. This challenging process requires advanced machine learning techniques, which can be computationally intensive. To overcome this, a new method has been developed that utilizes graph neural networks to efficiently identify particle clusters in real-time. This innovative approach leverages the distance matrix to create a more effective representation of particles, leading to improved clustering accuracy. To optimize performance, the method has been implemented on specialized hardware, the Xilinx UltraScale+ VCU 1525. Initial results demonstrate that the method outperforms existing solutions, achieving a 10% increase in accuracy while also reducing computation time by 25%. Furthermore, the method has been shown to process data at a rate of 40 kHz, significantly exceeding the requirements of the Belle II experiment. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize real-time particle reconstruction systems, paving the way for their use in future high-energy physics experiments. This research marks a significant milestone in the application of machine learning to real-time data processing, and its findings are expected to have a profound impact on the field. A significant risk factor for heart disease is coronary artery calcification (CAC), which can be detected through low-dose CT scans and quantified by the CAC score to assess heart attack risk. However, CAC volume measurements often vary significantly across repeated scans due to movement or repositioning during the procedure. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes generative models to create consistent and reliable CAC volume measurements. By leveraging the generative model, we can synthesize new images that accurately capture the CAC volume, and then use these synthesized images to refine the initial volume measurements, leading to more accurate and consistent results. In our study, we successfully applied this method to a dataset of 30 patients and observed a significant reduction in the variability of CAC volume measurements, from 34.6% to 8.1%. The results of our study demonstrate the potential of this method to improve the consistency and accuracy of CAC volume measurements, and we believe that this method can be further expanded to other imaging modalities and applications. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained significant attention as energy-efficient alternatives to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). To address this challenge, researchers have proposed the use of surrogate functions to approximate spike outputs, but this approach is limited by the difficulty of parameter tuning and the risk of gradient instability. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a novel regularization and normalization framework for surrogate gradient learning in SNNs, which is designed to improve the robustness and efficiency of training. The proposed method is evaluated on various benchmarks and shown to outperform previous approaches in terms of accuracy, energy efficiency, and model size. Notably, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MNIST dataset, demonstrating its potential for real-world applications. The study also provides insights into the effects of different surrogate functions on model performance and highlights the importance of regularization in achieving accurate results. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the training dynamics of SNNs and offers a practical solution for enhancing their performance in real-world applications. This paper investigates the effectiveness of using pre-trained speech models in detecting speaker gender from conversations where speakers overlap each other's speech. We examine the performance of two pre-trained models, wav2vec2.0 and WavLM, in two tasks: inferring speaker gender and determining speaker overlap. Our findings indicate that WavLM outperforms wav2vec2.0 in both tasks and achieves superior results in gender detection. Notably, we found that WavLM performs well even when the overlap between speakers is extensive, reaching accuracy rates of 0.65 and 0.61 on the TED and WSJ0 datasets respectively. Additionally, we observed that WavLM's performance is robust to varying levels of overlap between speakers. Furthermore, we analyzed the effect of different speech overlap durations on the model's accuracy and found that WavLM's performance is resilient to changes in overlap duration. Our results demonstrate that WavLM's pre-training on a large dataset of radio broadcasts contributes to its ability to handle conversations where speakers talk over each other. Overall, our study highlights the potential of using pre-trained speech models in detecting speaker gender and overlap in conversations. Monitoring ice field changes is crucial for understanding how these systems respond to climate change.  However, this process is complicated by the need for frequent updates due to rapidly melting glaciers.  To address this challenge, this research proposes a novel Bayesian deep learning approach that leverages SAR imagery to accurately map ice fields.  By integrating SAR imagery with existing ice field data, this method aims to improve monitoring efficiency.  The proposed Bayesian U-Net model utilizes a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to generate a posterior distribution of possible outputs, which are then combined to produce a final segmentation map.  This approach is tested on various SAR imagery sources and compared to traditional U-Net models, demonstrating its potential to improve monitoring of ice field changes.  The results show that the Bayesian U-Net model outperforms its competitors in terms of segmentation accuracy, especially when dealing with complex SAR imagery scenarios.  This method's ability to handle uncertainty in the output process also makes it a valuable tool for monitoring ice field changes. Through our work, we demonstrate the potential of equivariant graph attention networks to revolutionize molecular modeling and provide a foundation for the development of more advanced, spatially-aware graph neural networks. Predicting the trajectory of a moving object is a crucial task in robotics and transportation systems, but traditional methods often fall short by making unrealistic assumptions about the future path of a single target object. In contrast, real-world scenarios frequently involve multiple objects interacting with each other, making it essential to develop a predictive model that can handle multiple scenarios simultaneously. This paper proposes a novel approach called Multi-Scenario Trajectory Prediction (MSTP), which leverages a graph neural network to analyze the interactions among objects and generate multiple possible trajectories for various future scenarios. By incorporating a novel scenario graph and a multi-task loss function, MSTP is able to capture the complex relationships between objects and generate diverse trajectories. Experimental results demonstrate that MSTP outperforms existing methods in predicting multiple future scenarios. Furthermore, the approach's ability to generate diverse trajectories can be effectively utilized for applications such as trajectory planning and motion forecasting. Furthermore, we establish that near-optimal arm switches can be guaranteed even when arm values are unknown. We also demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms the standard Thompson sampling approach in this context. Finally, we conduct a simulation study to validate our theoretical claims and assess the algorithm's efficacy in real-world settings. This distribution is represented by a variational random attribute (VRA) kernel, which is composed of a base kernel and a set of conditional random attributes. The VRA kernel is learned through a combination of a base kernel and a set of conditional random attributes. The base kernel is learned using a meta-learning algorithm, which is trained on a large-scale dataset. This base kernel is then fine-tuned using a small set of labeled images. The conditional random attributes are learned using a variational autoencoder, which is trained to reconstruct the modified images. This approach enables the generation of images with desired attributes using a single model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on the CelebA dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results in attribute-based image manipulation. To improve the efficiency of intent prediction in conversational assistants, we propose an approach that leverages the guidance of relevant examples. Our method, called 'Example-Guided Intent Prediction with Observers', utilizes a set of supplementary 'observer' networks that analyze both the user's input and a selected reference example. By focusing on the most relevant features from the user's input and combining them with the reference example, the observer networks can generate a more accurate representation of the user's intent. This approach is particularly effective when training data is limited, as it enables the model to learn from the available examples more effectively. Our experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms existing methods in tasks with scarce training data, such as code completion and medical chatbots. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing code completion systems without requiring additional training data. Our research contributes to the field by introducing a novel method for intent prediction and providing a practical application of the observer networks in code completion systems. Our findings also highlight the potential of the observer networks to improve performance in code completion and medical chatbots. Accurate fire simulations rely on complex models that consider weather, terrain, and fuel factors. These models, however, are computationally expensive, hindering real-time predictions. By applying our method to a real-world wildfire case, we've successfully generated a simplified model that captures the dynamics of the original system, enabling efficient simulations. Our results show that this method can be used to make real-time predictions, offering a promising solution for the timely management of wildfire risks. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, we examine the concept of 'good enough' behavior, where agents settle for suboptimal outcomes in uncoordinated situations. This approach, known as "satisficing," is particularly relevant in environments where cooperation is not mandatory. By modeling the potential for coordination and using a linear programming framework, we establish a connection between satisficing and optimal strategies in uncertain scenarios. Our findings reveal that, even without explicit communication, certain multi-agent policies can be viewed as coordinated variants of optimal single-agent strategies. This insight offers a new perspective on multi-agent learning and may facilitate the development of decentralized learning techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, even in situations with no guaranteed coordination, certain stochastic games have equilibria that resemble optimal situations. This discovery provides a foundation for the development of decentralized learning techniques that can adapt to the ever-changing nature of multi-agent environments. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of decentralized learning and its relationship to optimal strategies in multi-agent settings. A widely used method for estimating causal effects through machine learning has been double machine learning (DML). Although DML has been successfully applied in various fields, including econometrics and public health, its use in causal mediation analysis has been limited until now. In this study, we develop a novel DML estimator for analyzing the indirect impact of treatments on outcomes through mediators. We also demonstrate the estimator's asymptotic properties and its robustness against model inaccuracies. Through simulations, we evaluate the estimator's performance under various scenarios and compare it with existing alternatives. Additionally, we apply this approach to a real-world dataset from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey to examine the relationship between body mass index and health outcomes, specifically cardiovascular disease risk, through the mediation of blood pressure. Our findings suggest that body mass index's effect on cardiovascular disease is significantly influenced by blood pressure. Furthermore, our approach offers greater efficiency and robustness against model inaccuracies compared to conventional linear regression-based mediation analysis. It also provides a more accurate estimation of body mass index's indirect effect than a widely used alternative based on ordinary least squares. Overall, our double machine learning-based estimator offers a more accurate estimation of causal mediation effects than existing methods. It can be applied in various fields, including public health, econometrics, and biostatistics. Monocular 3D object detection is a critical component of self-driving systems, but current methods have a significant drawback: they require a large number of ground-truth labels for training, which is both time-consuming and impractical due to the complexity of labeling 3D data. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that eliminates the need for these ground-truth labels by leveraging depth information. Our method involves a two-stage transmission network, where the first stage generates a message that contains depth-related information, and the second stage refines this message based on additional image data. This approach enables the detection of objects in complex urban environments, where depth estimation can be unreliable. To further improve performance, we also introduce a novel loss function that encourages the model to produce accurate depth estimates. Our method is the first to achieve state-of-the-art results on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark, and it outperforms other methods that rely on depth estimation, indicating its effectiveness. To facilitate further research in this area, we have made our code available for public use. We investigate the one-point distribution function of a critical one-dimensional polynuclear growth model, specifically focusing on the anisotropic model initially defined by Raz, Schehr, and Schehr in 2020. By employing a mapping onto a free fermion system, we derive an exact expression for the one-point distribution function, which is then generalized to include anisotropy. The resulting function is found to be determinantal in nature, with its kernel expressed as a sum over two distinct types of kernels, one corresponding to Raz, Schehr, and Schehr's original model and the other representing the anisotropic variant. The integration of video and language in multimedia content has become increasingly significant, particularly in the context of Chinese video understanding, where the limited availability of annotated data poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we introduce a novel pre-training method that leverages the concept of contrastive learning to enhance the representation of Chinese video and language. Our approach, which combines a video encoder with a language encoder, utilizes a unique contrastive loss function that encourages the model to identify and distinguish between semantically similar and dissimilar pairs of video and text inputs. Through this process, the model is effectively trained to recognize and prioritize meaningful connections between videos and language. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method in various downstream tasks, including video-text retrieval and video question answering, where the model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models. Seismic interpretation is a labor-intensive process that involves multiple iterations of experts' time, often limited by the availability of experienced interpreters. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Cooperative Inversion-Segmentation (CIS), which leverages deep learning to automatically generate high-quality seismic interpretations. CIS combines two interconnected modules: a segmentation module that identifies relevant seismic features and an inversion module that uses these features to create detailed interpretations. The segmentation module is trained using a novel loss function that incorporates a data-driven loss term to enhance its performance. Through a process of iterative refinement, CIS produces high-quality interpretations that are comparable to those created by experts. Our approach is evaluated using a large-scale dataset from the North Sea, where we demonstrate its ability to accurately identify faults and other structural features. The results show that CIS can effectively identify complex geological features, including fault zones, while also reducing the need for human intervention. The primary objective of visual saliency detection is to pinpoint the most relevant regions in an image that capture the human attention. However, the current state-of-the-art saliency detection models heavily rely on costly and time-consuming manual annotations. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel weakly-supervised approach that leverages a salient object subitizing (SOS) model. This model estimates the number of salient objects in an image, which is then utilized to refine the saliency map. To achieve this, we propose a salient object subitizing network (SOS-NET) that is trained using a unique dataset of images annotated with the number of salient objects. The SOS-NET is then integrated with a saliency detection model to produce a refined saliency map. Experimental results on five public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing weakly-supervised and deep learning-based methods. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the SOS-NET, highlighting its key benefits. The proposed approach is also compared to other weakly-supervised methods, showcasing its superiority. The code and models used in this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhouchanghuang/saliency_detection. Our approach is expected to pave the way for future research in weakly-supervised saliency detection. In contrast, our proposed method uses a similarity-based approach, leveraging a pre-trained classifier to identify similarities between input samples and known classes. By integrating an augmentation technique into the training process, our method is able to effectively identify unknown samples while maintaining high accuracy for known classes. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, our method's ability to generalize to unseen domains has been successfully demonstrated.
